title: SYSK Selects: How Daylight Saving Time Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of "How Daylight Savings Time Works" (originally published December 6, 2011), reintroduced by Chuck as a pick of the week. The hosts cover Benjamin Franklin's satirical daylight-saving letter to Paris and his compound-interest bequests, the spring-forward/fall-back rules, and how daylight saving time (DST) is set in the US by the Energy Policy Act of 2005 with exemptions for Arizona, Hawaii and Guam. They trace the history from George Vernon Hudson and William Willett's campaign, Germany's and Britain's World War I adoption, World War II, the Uniform Time Act of 1966, the 1973 oil-embargo extension, and Reagan's 1986 change. They weigh energy-savings studies, the golf and retail lobby, farmer opposition, traffic and crime claims, health effects (heart attacks, suicides, circadian disruption), Amtrak scheduling, and the Indiana studies. The episode closes with a contest announcement and a correction about patent trolls.

segments.title: Rerun intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as a Selects pick from December 6, 2011, tied to the recent fall-back clock change. The hosts begin with banter and then an anecdote about Benjamin Franklin's compound-interest bequests to Boston and Philadelphia.

segments.title: Franklin's daylight saving satire
segments.summary: The hosts describe Franklin's satirical 1784 letter as ambassador to France proposing waking Parisians earlier, which they say was dismissed as satire but planted an early seed of the idea.

segments.title: Spring forward, fall back rules
segments.summary: The hosts explain the mnemonic spring forward, fall back, and state the US rules: second Sunday in March to start and first Sunday in November to end, set by the Energy Policy Act of 2005. They note that Southern Hemisphere countries run the opposite schedule.

segments.title: US exemptions and global adoption
segments.summary: Arizona, Hawaii and Guam can opt out of US daylight saving time, and Indiana's mixed history is noted. The hosts cite a 2008 count of roughly 70 to 76 countries observing it and mention Japan, India and China as major industrialized non-observers. The European Union's standardized summertime dates are also discussed.

segments.title: Origins: Hudson and Willett
segments.summary: George Vernon Hudson, a New Zealand entomologist and astronomer, is named as the first to genuinely propose the idea. William Willett of England is credited more widely; he wrote The Waste of Daylight and lobbied Parliament, which rejected it in 1908, and he died before it was adopted.

segments.title: Wartime adoption and the Uniform Time Act
segments.summary: Germany first adopted daylight saving during World War I to save coal, and Britain and about thirty others followed. Many countries dropped it after the wars, and the US kept it year-round for three years during World War II. The Uniform Time Act of 1966 later set guidelines for states that chose to observe it.

segments.title: Oil embargo, Reagan extension, and energy savings debate
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1973 oil embargo extension that lengthened DST to eight months, and the 1986 change that moved the start to the first Sunday in April. They discuss the golf lobby's financial interest and studies showing only about a one percent energy saving, which critics challenge.

segments.title: Costs, benefits, and opposition
segments.summary: The hosts cover the arguments for and against: farmers' historical opposition, the claim of fewer traffic accidents and less crime, Skeptoid's view that the money motive dominates and the farmer claim is a myth, and airline and Amtrak scheduling problems. A recent Indiana study found a one percent rise in energy use.

segments.title: Health effects and circadian disruption
segments.summary: The hosts discuss circadian disruption described by a German chronobiologist, a Swedish study linking DST to heart attacks, and an Australian study linking the weeks after the change to male suicides among men with bipolar disorder. They close the topic with reflections on whether clock time is arbitrary.

segments.title: Contest announcement
segments.summary: The hosts announce a Facebook contest for an all-expenses-paid trip to Atlanta for US entrants, running through December third, with a referral prize.

segments.title: Correction about patent trolls
segments.summary: Josh corrects an earlier episode's description of patent trolls, explaining they buy patents without intent to manufacture and sue those who infringe. Listener contact details are given.
